$comment: Longer write-ups for some projects, keyed by project ID. Only entries with status "approved" appear on the site; drafts show up only in npm run preview:drafts. Every claim links to the project's repo at a fixed commit. reviewNotes are my own notes and never rendered.

caseStudies.problem: Work out a car's trajectory from KITTI Velodyne scans alone, with the code structured like a live sensor system: scans replayed at the timing they were captured, bounded memory between stages, and the result checked against ground truth.
caseStudies.approach: A producer thread loads a KITTI raw drive and releases the scans into a fixed-size queue at their original spacing. A consumer thread filters each scan, removes motion distortion using the OXTS velocity, and registers it against a running voxel map with KISS-ICP-style scan-to-map ICP. Poses are written in KITTI format, scored with relative pose error, and can be replayed live in an Open3D viewer.

pipeline.detail: DataLoader reads the Velodyne and OXTS frames; ReplayClock and ReplayScheduler release scans at their original capture times.
Fixed-size, thread-safe queue. The producer blocks when the consumer falls behind.
Drop invalid returns, range filter, voxel downsample.
Move every point to a single instant using the OXTS velocity and the point's capture offset.
Constant-velocity initial guess, adaptive correspondence threshold, robust Gauss-Newton against a voxel hash map.
KITTI-format trajectory, relative pose error against ground truth, Open3D playback.

decisions.title: Back-pressure instead of buffering
decisions.explanation: The stages are joined by a fixed-size queue. When odometry falls behind, the reader blocks instead of piling scans up in memory, so memory stays bounded on long drives.

evidence.note: Thread-safe bounded queue; push blocks while full

decisions.title: Prediction and an adaptive correspondence threshold
decisions.explanation: ICP for each scan starts from a constant-velocity prediction, which just applies the last relative motion again. The correspondence distance is three times an adaptive threshold, and that threshold is three times the RMS of recent model deviations (with a floor), so matching gets tighter when the motion is well predicted.

evidence.note: Constant-velocity prediction; max correspondence distance = 3 × kappa

decisions.title: Robust Gauss-Newton on a thread pool
decisions.explanation: Nearest-neighbour search and building the normal equations are split across a fixed pool of workers that is reused every iteration. Each thread keeps its own partial sums, so nothing needs a lock. Residuals go through a robust kernel, and each step is solved with an LDLT decomposition (up to 500 iterations, 1e-4 convergence).

evidence.note: ThreadPool, parallel correspondences, solveGaussNewton, ICP loop

decisions.title: Strict build and tests
decisions.explanation: C++20 with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror, unit and integration tests for every module (GoogleTest and CTest), AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and ThreadSanitizer presets, and a CI workflow.

evaluation.protocol: KITTI sequence 00, 4,541 evaluated poses (4,544 scans processed, none failed to load). Relative pose error between consecutive scans against KITTI odometry ground truth, converted to the Velodyne frame. Numbers are from the repository README.

limitations: This is odometry only. There's no loop closure or back-end optimization yet, so error grows with distance travelled.
The map drifts along with the trajectory. On loops you can see ghosting where the second pass doesn't line up with the first.
Nothing absolute (GPS/RTK or map matching) corrects the drift.
Only tested on one sequence (KITTI 00). The biggest error spike is at scan 2, where ICP starts from a zero-motion guess; the smaller ones line up with sharp turns.
nextSteps: Loop closure with a pose-graph back end
IMU fusion with an error-state Kalman filter
Absolute correction from GPS/RTK or a prior map
caseStudies.reproducibility: Build with the CMake presets (clang, C++20, Ninja), point src/config/dataset_config.json at a local copy of the KITTI raw data, then run run_odometry with --gt and --calib to print the metrics. The repository Quickstart has the details.

evidence.note: Repository at the time of writing (branch slam_stack)

reviewNotes: Title says SLAM but there's no loop closure yet. Publish this once loop closure is in and add ATE and drift numbers next to the RPE ones.
The rotation error plot recomputes 0.1090° while the README table says 0.110326°. Use one source.

caseStudies.problem: Given photos of an object taken from known camera positions, render it from viewpoints that were never photographed.
caseStudies.approach: This is my PyTorch implementation of NeRF (Mildenhall et al., 2020), trained on the Blender LEGO scene at 400×400. Each 3D point and viewing direction is positionally encoded and passed to two MLPs, a coarse one and a fine one (8 layers, 256 units, skip connection at layer 4). A pixel's colour comes from volume rendering along its camera ray: 64 stratified samples for the coarse network, then 128 more placed where the coarse network found density. I first trained it on a cloud A100 and later lost that model. The version here has the fixes described below and was retrained from scratch for 200,000 steps on my laptop's 6 GB RTX 3060, entirely in fp32.

pipeline.detail: Training images are loaded as RGBA and composited onto white, the same background the renderer assumes. They stay on the GPU.
1,024 random pixels per step. For the first 500 steps they only come from the central 50% of each image.
64 stratified samples per ray. Samples in cells the occupancy grid marks as empty skip the MLP.
128 extra samples drawn from the coarse weights, merged with the coarse ones and run through the fine MLP.
MSE on both the coarse and fine colours. Adam at 5e-4, decaying by 10× over 500,000 steps.
Deterministic renders of all 200 test views, scored with PSNR and SSIM.

decisions.title: Hierarchical sampling
decisions.explanation: The coarse network's weights along each ray act as a probability distribution, and the 128 fine samples are drawn from it, so the fine network spends its effort near surfaces. The fine sample positions are detached, as in the paper. My first version didn't do this, which let gradients from the fine network leak into the coarse one.

evidence.note: Fine samples drawn from detached weights

decisions.title: Skipping empty space with an occupancy grid
decisions.explanation: I wrote a 128³ occupancy grid over the cube [-1.5, 1.5]³. Every 16 steps it queries the coarse network's density and keeps a decaying maximum of each cell's opacity. Samples that land in empty cells skip both MLPs. In a 5,000-step test with everything else the same, the grid cut the time per step from 223 ms to 93 ms and ended at the same validation PSNR (23.19 dB with and without it), skipping about two thirds of all samples.

decisions.title: Keeping early training from collapsing
decisions.explanation: Short fp32 runs sometimes collapsed into a plain white image: the fine MLP's raw density went negative everywhere, so its ReLU passed no gradient and it never recovered. Two tricks from the paper and nerf-pytorch fixed it. One is a 500-step warm-up that samples only the middle of each image. The other is Gaussian noise (std 1.0) added to the raw density during training. With only the warm-up, one of three seeds still collapsed. With both, all three trained normally.

decisions.title: A fair background and repeatable scores
decisions.explanation: The first version's loader threw away the alpha channel, so it trained on black backgrounds while the renderer composited onto white. Now the ground truth is composited onto white as well. For evaluation, rendering has no jitter and the fine samples are placed deterministically, so scoring the same checkpoint twice gives exactly the same numbers.

decisions.title: Training that survives interruptions
decisions.explanation: A 7.5-hour run on a laptop needs to survive interruptions. Each checkpoint stores both models, the Adam state, the learning-rate schedule, the step, every RNG state, the config, the git commit and the occupancy grid. Checkpoints are written atomically, the newest three are kept, and --resume continues exactly where training stopped.

evaluation.protocol: All 200 test views of the Blender LEGO scene at 400×400. Each view is rendered deterministically, saved as an 8-bit PNG and scored against the ground truth composited onto white. PSNR is −10·log10(MSE) on RGB values in [0, 1]. SSIM uses an 11×11 Gaussian window with σ = 1.5, averaged over the RGB channels. The standard deviation across views is 1.35 dB for PSNR and 0.0051 for SSIM. I never used the test views for any decision during development; only three validation views were used for that.

limitations: One synthetic, object-centred scene with known camera poses. I haven't tried real photos yet.
Trained and scored at 400×400, half the resolution used in the NeRF paper, so these numbers can't be compared directly with published results.
Validation PSNR was still slowly rising at 200,000 steps (31.46 dB at the last check), so the model hasn't fully converged.
Rendering is slow: about 6 seconds per 400×400 image on the laptop GPU.
The first model's 29.90 dB isn't comparable with these numbers. That model is lost, so it could only be scored on four saved views against a black background.
nextSteps: Train for longer, since validation PSNR hadn't levelled off
Compare against Instant-NGP and 3D Gaussian Splatting on the same split, metrics and GPU
caseStudies.reproducibility: Put the Blender LEGO data in data/synthetic/lego/ and run ./run_lego.sh training.max_steps=200000. It trains, scores all 200 test views into outputs/v2/eval/metrics.json and renders the fly-around video. On a 6 GB laptop GPU it takes about 7.5 hours. docs/RESULTS.md in the repository has the unrounded numbers and the full scoring method.
reviewNotes: The project description also covers the SfM pipeline, which lives in a separate repo (SfM-CV) that isn't linked yet. Link it here once its PnP/BA fixes are done.

caseStudies.problem: Plan smooth, collision-free paths for a car-like vehicle on an occupancy grid. Plain grid A* gives paths a car can't follow, because a car can't turn on the spot.
caseStudies.approach: A ROS 2 package with three nodes. A Python node publishes the map, start and goal. A C++ node runs Hybrid A* over continuous (x, y, heading) states, binned by heading, expanding forward and reverse motion primitives from a bicycle model. A second Python node animates the planned path.

pipeline.detail: env_publisher.py publishes /map, /start and /goal.
Dijkstra flood fill over the grid from the goal, so the cost-to-go accounts for obstacles.
Expand motion primitives (2.5 m wheelbase, 0.45 rad max steer, 1 m steps) forwards and in reverse, checking for collisions at sub-steps along each primitive.
Publish /planned_path; path_viz.py animates it.

decisions.title: Cost terms that favour drivable paths
decisions.explanation: Edge costs penalize reversing, switching direction, steering hard and changing the steering angle. That pushes the search towards smooth forward motion while still allowing reverse moves like parking.

decisions.title: A heuristic that knows about obstacles
decisions.explanation: A Dijkstra flood fill from the goal gives a cost-to-go that goes around obstacles, instead of plain straight-line distance.

limitations: Shown on one synthetic map; there are no runtime or success-rate numbers yet.
config/params.yaml is never loaded, so the planner runs with the constants in planner.hpp (kReverseCost = 10.0 rather than the YAML's reverse_penalty of 1.5).
nextSteps: Reeds-Shepp analytic expansion to the goal pose (declared in the planner but not implemented yet)
Use the obstacle k-d tree for collision checks
caseStudies.reproducibility: Build with colcon on ROS 2 Humble with OMPL installed, then run: ros2 launch hybrid_astar astar_viz_launch.py
reviewNotes: Rewrite against the new commit once Reeds-Shepp, smoothing and parameter loading are in. The site description already mentions smoothing and Reeds-Shepp.

caseStudies.problem: Label every pixel of a KITTI street image as one of the 19 Cityscapes classes, such as road, car, building or vegetation, with only 200 labelled images to learn from.
caseStudies.approach: A UNet I wrote from scratch in PyTorch: a four-level encoder (64 to 512 channels, two 3×3 convolutions with batch norm per level) and a transposed-convolution decoder with skip connections. No pretrained weights. The 200 labelled KITTI images are split once into 160 for training and 40 for validation, and the split is saved in the repo. The first version (v1) trained on all 34 KITTI label IDs at 256×512. The second (v2) trains on the 19 classes that are scored, at 352×1184, and was trained from scratch for 600 epochs on my laptop's 6 GB RTX 3060, in fp32.

pipeline.detail: The 34 KITTI label IDs are mapped to the 19 trainIds with a lookup table. Everything else becomes 255 and is ignored. Images are resized once to 352×1184 and kept in RAM.
Random scale between 0.75 and 1.5, a random 352×592 crop, flips, brightness, contrast, colour jitter and blur.
Batch 4, plain cross-entropy that skips ignored pixels, AdamW at 1e-3 with 5 warm-up epochs and then poly decay to 0.
Every 5 epochs on the 40 val images. best.pt is saved when val mIoU goes up and last.pt every epoch, so a run can resume.
Predict at 352×1184, upsample the logits to the original image size and add every image to one 19×19 confusion matrix.

decisions.title: Scoring it the standard way
decisions.explanation: The v1 training loop averaged mIoU over batches of 12 images, which drags the mean down whenever a class is rare in a batch. Its plots showed about 0.28. I wrote evaluate.py to build one confusion matrix over the whole val split at the original resolution and average IoU over the 19 classes, and tested the metric against a small example worked out by hand. Scored this way, the same v1 checkpoint gets 0.364.

decisions.title: Training on the scored classes at KITTI's image shape
decisions.explanation: v1 predicted all 34 label IDs and squashed the roughly 1242×375 images into 256×512. v2 predicts only the 19 classes that are scored and resizes to 352×1184, which keeps the aspect ratio. To fit in 6 GB it trains on random 352×592 crops after random scaling. Thin and small classes improved the most: at the last epoch of each run, traffic signs went from 0.200 to 0.425 IoU and poles from 0.369 to 0.442. I changed the classes, resolution, crops and schedule together, so I can't say how much each one helped.

decisions.title: Learning-rate schedule and checkpoints
decisions.explanation: v1 used Adam at a fixed 1e-3 and only the last checkpoint. v2 uses AdamW with 5 warm-up epochs and poly decay (power 0.9), stepped every batch, and checks val mIoU every 5 epochs. The best checkpoint is picked on the same 40 images it's scored on, so the main number I report is the last epoch's.

decisions.title: Measuring speed before changing it
decisions.explanation: I timed the training step with each usual speed-up added one at a time. Caching images in RAM and pinned memory changed nothing, because the step is all GPU compute. channels_last and torch.compile made it slower on this GPU. bf16 was about 2.2× faster, but I kept v2 in fp32 so it matches v1. A 600-epoch run took 4 h 33 min, 26.3 s per epoch.

evaluation.protocol: 40 validation images held out from the 200 labelled KITTI semantics images (splits/val.txt). KITTI's test labels aren't public, so there's no test-server score. Predictions are upsampled to the original image size and all 40 images go into one 19×19 confusion matrix. IoU = TP / (TP + FP + FN) for each class, averaged over the 19 classes. Checkpoint last.pt, epoch 600 of 600.
Same 40 validation images and confusion matrix as above. Correct pixels over all labelled pixels; ignored pixels aren't counted.
Same method, checkpoint best.pt from epoch 500. It was picked on the same 40 images it's scored on, so it's a bit optimistic. After about epoch 450 val mIoU moves between 0.39 and 0.405.

evaluation.metric: Mean IoU, v1 (last epoch, scored again)
evaluation.protocol: The first model, epoch 500 of 500, scored with the same method on the same 40 images. It predicts 34 label IDs, which go through the same mapping to the 19 classes; a pixel predicted as an ignored ID counts as a miss.

limitations: Only 40 validation images, taken from the KITTI training set, and no test-server score. Neighbouring checkpoints differ by about 0.01 mIoU, so smaller differences are noise.
Trained from scratch on 160 images. People, riders and bicycles are still almost always wrong (IoU under 0.1), and bus, train and motorcycle have too few pixels in the val split to score reliably.
nextSteps: A pretrained encoder (for example ResNet-34) in place of the from-scratch one
bf16 training, which measured about 2.2× faster on the same GPU
caseStudies.reproducibility: Put the KITTI semantics data under data/ as the README describes and install requirements.txt. EPOCHS=600 bash run_v2.sh runs the tests, scores the v1 checkpoints again, trains v2 and evaluates it. python evaluate.py outputs/v2/checkpoints/best.pt outputs/v2/checkpoints/last.pt prints 0.4051 and 0.3997.
